claims.text: A predictive model incorporating chemical-disorder and local-lattice-distortion descriptors will identify low-lattice-thermal-conductivity high-entropy alloys more accurately than current models.
Current predictive models rely on averaged or phase-pure material parameters.
Conventional average-property models tend to overestimate phonon thermal conductivity in highly disordered HEAs.
Equiatomic FeCoCrMnNi is a chemically disordered, single-phase random-solid-solution HEA.
CoCrFeNiCu is an example of a single-phase HEA with substantial chemical disorder.
The proposed HEAs exhibit moderate atomic-size mismatch.
The predictive approach is applicable when synthesis produces a homogeneous, chemically disordered solid solution.
Multiphase precipitation, clustering, or ordering limits the applicability of the predictive approach.
Strong chemical disorder produces atomic-mass and force-constant fluctuations in FeCoCrMnNi.
Chemical disorder and local lattice distortion create a heterogeneous force-constant landscape.
Mass and force-constant fluctuations scatter phonons and reduce their lifetimes or mean free paths.
The proposed model captures nonlinear interactions among contributions from the constituent elements.
Accounting for mass and force-constant fluctuations yields lower predicted phonon thermal conductivity than homogeneous average-property models.
Alloys selected by the approach will have measured lattice thermal conductivity more than 20–30% below values predicted by conventional models.
Lower lattice thermal conductivity will improve the alloys' thermal-insulation performance.
Strong short-range ordering or phase separation will diminish model accuracy when those heterogeneities are not represented by the random-disorder descriptors.
Laser-flash analysis or time-domain thermoreflectance can be used to determine the alloys' lattice thermal conductivity.
Inelastic neutron or X-ray scattering can characterize the phonon density of states or lattice dynamics of an HEA.
Less than 20% improvement over conventional predictions is designated as a falsifying outcome.
Unexpected phase separation or ordering is designated as a falsifying outcome.

contradictions.description: Phase separation and ordering are defined as conditions outside the model's applicability, but their occurrence is also treated as falsifying the in-domain hypothesis. An out-of-domain specimen should ordinarily invalidate the test rather than falsify the model's claim for homogeneous disordered solid solutions.
